resources.title: Language and structure techniques
resources.summary: The language and structure techniques to name in a reading answer, each with an example written for this page and the effect to write about, because naming a technique earns nothing on its own.

sources.name: AQA GCSE English Language specification (8700)
sources.where: AO2, and Papers 1 and 2 Section A

resources.statusNote: AO2 asks you to analyse "how writers use language and structure to achieve effects", "using relevant subject terminology". The term is the start; the effect on the reader is the mark.

blocks.title: Language
rows: Simile
the fog crept in like a thief
compares directly, so the reader brings the feel of one thing to the other: here, threat and secrecy
Metaphor
the corridor was a throat, swallowing us
says one thing *is* another, which is stronger than a simile
Personification
the wind howled at the door
gives a thing human feelings, making the setting seem alive or hostile
Pathetic fallacy
rain hammered on the day of the funeral
weather that matches a mood, so the setting reflects what a character feels
Alliteration
the cold, cruel cliffs
repeated opening sounds that make a phrase stand out; a hard *c* sounds harsh
Sibilance
the sea sighed and hissed on the sand
repeated *s* sounds: soft and soothing, or sinister
Onomatopoeia
the gate clanged shut
a word that sounds like its meaning, so the reader hears the moment
Semantic field
battle, wounded, retreat, in a story about a school
a group of words from one area that builds an idea: school as a war
Rhetorical question
How much longer can we ignore this?
makes the reader think for themselves, and the answer feels obvious
Direct address
You know this is wrong.
speaks to the reader as *you*, so they feel involved
Rule of three
cheap, fast and dangerous
three items that sound complete and are easy to remember
Hyperbole
I have told you a million times
deliberate exaggeration, for emphasis or humour
Statistics and facts
four in five pupils agree
make an argument sound objective and hard to dismiss

blocks.title: Structure
rows: Shift in focus
from a crowded street to one face in a window
guides where the reader looks, like a camera zooming in
Flashback
a return to the character's childhood
fills in the past to explain the present
Foreshadowing
an early hint of what will happen
builds tension, because the reader expects something
Short sentence
He was gone.
stops the reader after longer sentences, for shock or finality
One-line paragraph
a single sentence set apart
makes a key moment stand out
Cyclical structure
the ending returns to the opening image
gives a sense of completion, or of being trapped
Contrast
a warm kitchen, then the frozen yard
sharpens both halves by putting them side by side

blocks.body: **A paragraph that scores.** Name the technique, quote it, then explain the effect on the reader with a precise verb: *The simile "crept in like a thief" makes the fog seem deliberate and threatening, as if the town is about to be robbed.*

applications.title: Adverts
applications.body: An advert that says *you deserve it* uses direct address; *pure, natural, delicious* is a rule of three. Spotting the technique shows how it is trying to persuade you.

applications.title: Speeches
applications.body: Political speeches lean on rhetorical questions and the rule of three because they are easy to remember and sound certain when spoken aloud.
